The Amand material is ALREADY heavily ingested: 198 nodes carry the 'amand1945' tag (86 argument, 11 concept, ~99 synthesis, 2 publication). The brief assumed no publication node existed; in fact there are two (duplicates). Therefore I propose NO new publication_node. DUPLICATE PUBLICATION NODES. 'pub_amand_1945_fatalisme' (label: Fatalisme et liberté dans l'antiquité grecque; metadata year 1945, author 'David Amand', Louvain, Bibliothèque de l'Université, ISBN 9789025606466) and 'pub_amand_1973_fatalisme_liberte' (label: Amand de Mendieta, Fatalisme et liberté... (1973); metadata year 1973, author 'Emmanuel Amand de Mendieta', Hakkert Amsterdam, SAME ISBN 9789025606466, with first_edition={1945, Louvain}). These are the SAME monograph: 1945 Louvain first edition (thesis defended 1944) vs 1973 Hakkert photo-reprint. Identical ISBN proves it. RECOMMENDATION FOR HUMAN: merge into one canonical node. Suggest keeping 'pub_amand_1945_fatalisme' (correct first-edition year and the year used in every node tag 'amand1945'), folding the 1973 reprint into its metadata (reprint: {year:1973, publisher:'Hakkert, Amsterdam'}), and re-pointing the single edge currently on pub_amand_1973 (authored_by) plus the alternative_names ['Amand 1973','Amand de Mendieta 1973']. The 1973 node's local_path_hint points to the on-disk PDF/MD.

AUTHOR NAME / YEAR DISCREPANCY (requested by brief). The tag 'amand1945' / 'Amand 1945' is CORRECT for the first edition: David Amand (religious name of Emmanuel Amand de Mendieta, O.S.B.), 'Fatalisme et liberté dans l'antiquité grecque: recherches sur la survivance de l'argumentation morale antifataliste de Carnéade chez les philosophes grecs et les théologiens chrétiens des quatre premiers siècles', Louvain, Bibliothèque de l'Université (Recueil de travaux d'histoire et de philologie, 3e sér., fasc. 19), 1945. The on-disk source the KG cites is the 1973 Amsterdam (Hakkert) photographic REPRINT — same pagination, same text, author now styled 'Emmanuel Amand de Mendieta'. Title page of the reprint still reads 'DAVID AMAND ... 1973'. So 1945 (content) and 1973 (the physical copy on disk) are both legitimate; they are NOT an error, they are first-edition vs reprint. Page numbers cited as 'p. NN' in node descriptions match BOTH editions (reprint preserves pagination).

EXISTING WIRING of amand1945 arguments uses 'authored_by -> scholar_amand_de_mendieta_e' (the PERSON node, 29 edges) to mark provenance. This is an ontology stretch (authored_by normally targets a work, and here it conflates 'Amand reconstructs this' with 'X authored this'). Separately, only pub_amand_1945_fatalisme carries 8 'cites_primary_source' + 11 'discusses' edges. The clean fix is the source_for/discussed_in edges proposed below, pointing the floating arguments to the publication node rather than (or in addition to) the scholar person node. Flagging for human: decide whether to retire the 29 authored_by->scholar edges once source_for edges land.

label: The Carneadean Anti-Astrology / Anti-Fatalist Tradition
description: The transmission tradition reconstructed by David Amand (1945): a coherent set of moral and anti-astrological arguments originating in Carneades' anti-Stoic, anti-mantic polemic (2nd c. BCE), transmitted in writing by his pupil Clitomachus, and surviving—often as a recognizable cluster of topoi (the impossibility of an exact horoscope, the twins, the collective death of those born under different stars, the nomima barbarika / barbarian customs, the animals also subject to astral fate, plus the moral arguments that fatalism abolishes praise/blame, legislation, piety and prayer)—through Cicero (De Divinatione, De Fato), Philo (De Providentia), Pseudo-Plutarch (De Fato), Aetius, Favorinus (via Gellius), Bardaisan (Liber legum regionum), Firmicus Maternus (Mathesis I, reported as the adversaries' arguments), Origen (Philocalia 23 = Comm. in Gen. III; Contra Celsum), Eusebius (Praeparatio Evangelica VI.6, 8, 10–11), Basil (Hexaemeron VI.5–7), Gregory of Nyssa (Contra Fatum; De Hom. Opif.; Oratio Catechetica 31), Diodore of Tarsus (Contra Fatum/astrologos), John Chrysostom, Nemesius of Emesa (De Natura Hominis 35–38), and others. Amand's central thesis: these patristic 'witnesses' are not independent but preserve, with varying fidelity and progressive decay, the same Carneadean dossier, with Origen as the pivot through which the philosophical arguments were transposed into a Christian theological key.
evidence: Amand 1945, whole monograph; see esp. Intro §II ch. II (Carneades' arguments, pp. 45-61) and the witness chapters of Livre II; synthesis nodes synthesis_amand1945_origen_pivot_witness, synthesis_amand1945_cappadocian_chain, synthesis_amand1945_three_six_witnesses_rule already encode this thesis. NB distinct from debate_stoic_academic_hellenistic (the broader Stoic-vs-Academic fate controversy) — this node is specifically the diachronic SURVIVAL/transmission of one argument-dossier.

rationale: Amand 1945 is the monograph that reconstructs and names this tradition; the debate node is essentially the subject of the book.
source_file: Amand de Mendieta 1973 (reprint of 1945), Fatalisme et liberté dans l'antiquité grecque

rationale: Carneades is the originator of the argument-dossier per Amand.
Clitomachus is, for Amand, the written transmitter of Carneades' otherwise unwritten theses (synthesis_amand1945_clitomachus_transmission_carneadean_theses).
Cicero (De Div. II, De Fato) is Amand's principal Latin indirect transmitter of the Carneadean arguments.
Philo's De Providentia I.77-88 is Amand's textus testis n°1 (witness n°1) of the Carneadean moral dossier.
Origen is Amand's pivot witness, transposing the philosophical arguments into a Christian theological key (synthesis_amand1945_origen_pivot_witness).
source_file: Amand 1945, Livre II ch. on Origen

rationale: Eusebius PE VI.6/8/10-11 is Amand's witness n°4; preserves long Carneadean extracts (incl. Bardaisan's nomima barbarika).
Basil Hexaemeron VI.5-7 is Amand's own starting point (synthesis_amand1945_basil_hex_vi_7_amand_origin_point); deploys two Carneadean topoi.
Gregory of Nyssa (Contra Fatum, Oratio Catech. 31, De Hom. Opif.) is a secondary double witness in Amand's reconstruction.
Diodore of Tarsus' Contra Fatum is, for Amand, the largest anti-fatalist treatise with two Carneadean echoes (synthesis_amand1945_diodore_tarsus_*).
Nemesius De Nat. Hom. 35-38 gives a skeletal late summary; Amand judges the dossier 'decayed' here (synthesis_amand1945_nemesius_witness_decay).
Chrysostom (Hom. post reditum Gothi 6 = witness n°5; Hom. 1 Tim 1.3) preserves one of the two most detailed Greek Christian versions of the moral dossier.
Bardaisan (Liber legum regionum) is Amand's crucial secondary witness who amplifies the nomima barbarika topos ethnographically.
source_file: Amand 1945, ARGUMENT DES νόμιμα βαρβαρικά, pp. 57-59

rationale: Firmicus Mathesis I.2 reports, as the adversaries' objections, the Carneadean dossier (witness n°3); paradox: a pagan astrologer preserving the anti-astrology arguments.
Favorinus' 14 anti-astrological arguments (via Gellius NA XIV.1) are a loose neo-Academic redeployment of the Carneadean dossier.
Amand's transmission chain Carneades -> (Clitomachus) -> Cicero (synthesis_amand1945_transmission_carneades_to_philo_chain).
Amand argues a four-century filiation Carneades -> Origen (synthesis_amand1945_origen_carneadean_filiation), mediated chiefly through Cicero's De Fato/De Nat. Deor.
Cappadocian chain Origen -> Basil (synthesis_amand1945_cappadocian_chain; synthesis_amand1945_basil_origen_christian_insertion).
Cappadocian chain Origen -> Gregory of Nyssa (synthesis_amand1945_cappadocian_chain).
Amand holds Eusebius a faithful disciple of Origen on free will (synthesis_amand1945_eus_dependence_origen).
Amand (following Wendland) traces Philo's De Providentia anti-astrology back to a Carneadean / neo-Academic source (synthesis_amand1945_transmission_carneades_to_philo_chain).

author: Cicero

author: Cicero
critical_edition: Cicero, De Divinatione, ed. R. Giomini, Teubner (Leipzig, 1975); ed. A.S. Pease (Urbana, 1920–23)
note: Dilemmatic anti-divination argument: 'ubi est igitur ista divinatio Stoicorum? ...'. Latin text NOT verbatim in the Amand OCR at the point I read (Amand gives a French paraphrase in the note); ingest from a Cicero critical edition. found_verbatim:false for the original text.

author: Cicero
locus: Book III (Cotta's Academic critique, esp. III.20–93)
critical_edition: Cicero, De Natura Deorum, ed. O. Plasberg–W. Ax, Teubner (Leipzig, 1933); ed. A.S. Pease (Cambridge MA, 1955–58)
cited_by: Amand 1945, p. 45 (Intro §II ch. II §III in fine)
note: Amand draws the Carneadean denial of cosmic teleology and the Stoic proofs of god's existence from the Academic (Carneadean) material in Cicero De Nat. Deor. III; work node work_de_natura_deorum_cicero exists in KG.

author: Cicero
locus: II.43.89–47.99 (esp. II.46.97 on the rapidity of the celestial revolution)
critical_edition: Cicero, De Divinatione, ed. R. Giomini, Teubner (1975); cf. also the Carneadean material at Sextus Empiricus, Adv. Math. V (Contra astrologos), ed. H. Mutschmann, Teubner
note: Anti-astrological argument I. Amand's primary witnesses for the five topoi are Cicero De Div. II and Sextus Empiricus Adv. Math. V; he also adduces Firmicus and the patristic chain. Multiple loci — ingest De Div. II.43-47 first.

author: Cicero
locus: II.43.90 (the twins / 'Proci' argument); parallel Sextus Empiricus Adv. Math. V.95–105
critical_edition: Cicero, De Divinatione, ed. R. Giomini, Teubner (1975); Sextus Empiricus, Adversus Mathematicos V, ed. H. Mutschmann (Teubner) / R.G. Bury (Loeb)
note: Anti-astrological argument II (same constellation, different destinies — 'pourquoi pas plusieurs Homères, plusieurs Socrates'). Standard Carneadean topos.

author: Cicero
locus: II.47.97 (collective death; Roman examples Cannae, etc.); parallel Sextus Empiricus Adv. Math. V.91–94
critical_edition: Cicero, De Divinatione, ed. R. Giomini, Teubner (1975); Sextus Empiricus, Adversus Mathematicos V, ed. H. Mutschmann (Teubner)
note: Anti-astrological argument III. Amand: at Carneades it rests on Roman examples (Cannae, the wreck at the Piraeus). The patristic counterpart (collective death) is already grounded for some witnesses (Eusebius PE VI); the Carneadean root locus is Cicero De Div. II / Sextus.

author: Firmicus Maternus / Bardaisan (Eusebius)
work: Mathesis I.2.1–4 (adversaries' statement of the argument) ; cf. Bardaisan Liber legum regionum in Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica VI.10.1–48
locus: Firmicus, Mathesis I.2.1–4 ; Eusebius PE VI.10.1–48
critical_edition: Firmicus Maternus, Matheseos libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll – F. Skutsch, I (Teubner, Leipzig 1897), p. 6 l.1 – p. 7 l.8 ; Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelica I-X, ed. G. Dindorf, I (Teubner, Leipzig 1867), pp. 314-323 (= PG 21, 464B–477B); Bardaisan, Liber legum regionum, ed. F. Nau, Patrologia Syriaca I.2 (Paris 1907), col. 490-657
cited_by: Amand 1945, pp. 55-60 (Intro §II ch. II §V.4); the Firmicus Latin block is quoted verbatim by Amand at p. 57
note: Anti-astrological argument IV (νόμιμα βαρβαρικά). Amand quotes the Firmicus Latin in extenso (see the quote record below, found_verbatim:true). Bardaisan's amplified version is preserved in Eusebius PE VI.10 (= work also feeding the Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions IX.19-28 and Ps.-Caesarius). concept_nomima_barbarika_amand exists.

author: Cicero / Sextus Empiricus
work: Sextus Empiricus, Adversus Mathematicos V (Contra astrologos); cf. Cicero De Div. II
locus: Sextus Empiricus Adv. Math. V.103–105 (the ass/man born under the same degree)
critical_edition: Sextus Empiricus, Adversus Mathematicos V, ed. H. Mutschmann (Teubner) / R.G. Bury (Loeb, vol. IV); Cicero De Div. II ed. Giomini (Teubner 1975)
note: Anti-astrological argument V: animals are equally subject to astral fate (the pivotal image of an ass and a man born under the same zodiacal degree). Sextus is the clearest verbatim witness.

author: Philo of Alexandria
critical_edition: Philo, De Providentia, ed. J.B. Aucher (Venice 1822), I, pp. 39-40 (Armenian + Latin); cf. P. Wendland, Philos Schrift über die Vorsehung (Berlin 1892); SC 35bis (Hadas-Lebel 1973) for the modern critical text
note: Witness n°1. Survives mainly in Armenian (Aucher); Wendland reconstructed the neo-Academic/Carneadean origin. The four sub-arguments (moral responsibility I.78-83; ethnic customs I.84-86; collective death I.87; conception moment I.87) are separate nodes below.

author: Philo of Alexandria
critical_edition: Philo, De Providentia, ed. J.B. Aucher (Venice 1822), I; cf. P. Wendland 1892; SC 35bis
note: Philo's first and (for Amand) strongest anti-fatalist argument: fatalism abolishes moral responsibility.

author: Philo of Alexandria
critical_edition: Philo, De Providentia, ed. J.B. Aucher (Venice 1822), I, pp. 39-40; cf. P. Wendland 1892, pp. 30-32; SC 35bis
cited_by: Amand 1945, p. 85 (OCR ll. 5403-5419); explicit edition cite at p. 58 n.1 'PHILON, Περὶ προνοίας, 1, 84-86, éd. I.B. AUCHER, I, p. 39-40'
note: Philonian nomima barbarika argument (Jews: circumcision, sabbath, food laws; Scythians [Amand: perhaps read Persians] incest; Egyptians zoolatry).

author: Philo of Alexandria
critical_edition: Philo, De Providentia, ed. J.B. Aucher (Venice 1822), I; SC 35bis
note: Philonian collective-death argument (sack of a city, plague). Amand judges it merely sketched ('simplement esquissé').

author: Philo of Alexandria
critical_edition: Philo, De Providentia, ed. J.B. Aucher (Venice 1822), I; SC 35bis
note: Philonian form of the impossibility-of-exact-observation argument, transferred to the moment of conception.

author: Origen
work: Philocalia 23 (= Commentary on Genesis III, on Gen. 1:14)
critical_edition: Origène, Philocalie 21-27 (Sur le libre arbitre), ed. É. Junod, SC 226 (Paris: Cerf, 1976); J.A. Robinson, The Philocalia of Origen (Cambridge 1893), pp. 202-205
note: Origen's thesis: stars are σημαντικοί (significative) not ποιητικοί (efficient causes); four aligned arguments. SC 226 (Junod) is on disk per CLAUDE.md (SC 226 RTF).

author: Origen
critical_edition: Origène, Philocalie 21-27, ed. É. Junod, SC 226 (Cerf 1976); J.A. Robinson, The Philocalia of Origen (Cambridge 1893), pp. 206-207
note: Origen distinguishes the abstract νοητὸν δωδεκατημόριον (zodiacal sign) from the visible μόρφωμα (constellation) and invokes the precession of the equinoxes (Hipparchus). Amand stresses its exceptional scientific-philological significance.

author: Nemesius of Emesa
critical_edition: Nemesius, De Natura Hominis, ed. M. Morani, Teubner (Leipzig 1987); PG 40, 504-817 (text Amand cites)
note: Skeletal summary of the Carneadean moral dossier (5 absurd consequences of astral fatalism). Morani is now the standard critical edition; Amand cited PG 40.

author: Nemesius of Emesa
critical_edition: Nemesius, De Natura Hominis, ed. M. Morani, Teubner (1987); PG 40
note: Theological 'blasphemy' argument: the stars themselves are unjust, and God responsible for crimes, if he made stars that necessitate them. Amand: 'plutôt théologique'.

author: Nemesius of Emesa
critical_edition: Nemesius, De Natura Hominis, ed. M. Morani, Teubner (1987); PG 40
note: Peripatetic refutation of the Egyptian astrologers who admit astral heimarmene yet claim apotropaic rites can avert it.

author: Nemesius of Emesa
critical_edition: Nemesius, De Natura Hominis, ed. M. Morani, Teubner (1987); PG 40
note: Peripatetic critique (via Nemesius' source) of the Middle-Platonist conditional-heimarmene theory typified by Pseudo-Plutarch Peri heimarmenes. Links to concept_heimarmene_conditional_amand1945.

author: Gregory of Nyssa
critical_edition: Gregory of Nyssa, Oratio Catechetica Magna, ed. J.H. Srawley (Cambridge 1903), pp. 113-114; also SC 453 (R. Winling, 2000); PG 45, 9-105
note: Gregory's moral Carneadean argument as a school topos (free will is the precondition of virtue; without it praise/blame collapse).

author: John Chrysostom
work: Homilia habita postquam presbyter Gothus concionatus fuerat (Hom. post reditum Gothi)
critical_edition: PG 63, 499-510 (no modern SC critical edition of this homily; Amand cites Migne)
note: Amand's 'textus testis n°5' — one of the two most detailed Greek Christian versions of the Carneadean moral dossier (5 structured arguments).

author: John Chrysostom
work: Homiliae in epistulam I ad Timotheum, Hom. 1 (on 1 Tim 1:3)
critical_edition: PG 62, 501-600 (Amand cites Migne; no SC critical edition)
note: Chrysostom's 'first text': reductio ad absurdum — if heimarmene/genesis rules, abandon all activity (don't sow, don't plant, don't soldier).

author: Favorinus of Arelate (via Aulus Gellius)
critical_edition: Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae, ed. P.K. Marshall, OCT (Oxford 1968), vol. II; cf. ed. C. Hosius, Teubner (1903)
note: Favorinus' 10th anti-astrological argument: it is intolerable that the Chaldaeans subject even the soul's volitions, desires and aversions to the stars (the will-to-bathe example).

author: Aristotle (Amand's pre-Carneadean anti-fatalist) / reported tradition
work: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics III; cf. De Interpretatione 9
locus: EN III.5 (1113b–1114a, on praise/blame and the practice of legislators)
critical_edition: Aristotle, Ethica Nicomachea, ed. I. Bywater, OCT (Oxford 1894); De Interpretatione ed. L. Minio-Paluello, OCT (1949)
cited_by: Amand 1945 (Intro, on Aristotle as 'the most complete pre-Carneadean anti-fatalist')
note: Aristotelian anticipation: legislators' practice of reward/punishment presupposes that we are causes of our actions. EN III.5 is the canonical locus (νομοθέται κολάζουσι); Amand treats Aristotle as the principal pre-Carneadean source. Locus is my philological judgement, not an explicit Amand page cite for this exact sub-node — HUMAN VERIFY.

text_original: Si stellarum mixturis mores hominibus coloresque tribuuntur, et, quasi quodam picturae genere atque artificio, stellarum cursus mortalium corporum liniamenta componunt, id est si Luna facit candidos, Mars rubeos, Saturnus nigros, cur omnes in Aethiopia nigri, in Germania candidi, in Thracia rubei procreantur, quasi Luna et Mars in Aethiopia uim suam uiresque non habeant, et potestatem suam fingendique licentiam in Germania ac Thracia Saturni deserat stella?
translation_en: If men's characters and complexions are assigned by the mixtures of the stars, and the courses of the stars compose the lineaments of mortal bodies as by a kind of pictorial art and craft — that is, if the Moon makes (people) white, Mars red, Saturn black — why are all in Ethiopia born black, in Germany white, in Thrace ruddy, as though the Moon and Mars did not exert their force and power in Ethiopia, and the star of Saturn abandoned its power and licence of shaping in Germany and Thrace?
author: Firmicus Maternus
critical_edition: Firmicus Maternus, Matheseos libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll – F. Skutsch, vol. I (Teubner, Leipzig 1897), p. 6 l.1 – p. 7 l.8
cited_by: Amand 1945, p. 57 (quoted verbatim in the OCR of the 1973 reprint, ll. ~4051-4090)

text_original: Scythae soli inmanis feritatis crudelitate grassantur, Itali fiunt regali semper nobilitate praefulgidi, Galli stolidi, leues Graeci, Afri subdoli, auari Syri, acuti Siculi, luxuriosi semper Asiani et uoluptatibus occupati, Hispani elata iactantiae animositate praeposteri.
translation_en: The Scythians alone rage with the cruelty of monstrous savagery; the Italians are ever resplendent with regal nobility; the Gauls dull, the Greeks fickle, the Africans crafty, the Syrians greedy, the Sicilians sharp, the Asians ever luxurious and given over to pleasures, the Spaniards perverse with the puffed-up spirit of boastfulness.
author: Firmicus Maternus
critical_edition: Firmicus Maternus, Matheseos libri VIII, ed. W. Kroll – F. Skutsch, vol. I (Teubner, Leipzig 1897), p. 6-7
note: The ethnographic catalogue (each nation's fixed character) that grounds the nomima barbarika argument: whole peoples share a character regardless of individual horoscopes, refuting astral determinism of character.

author: Carneades (Amand's reconstruction; phrase as transmitted)
critical_edition: Amand 1945, pp. 55-60; cf. F. Boll, 'Die νόμιμα βαρβαρικά als Beweis gegen die Astrologie' (cited by Amand)
cited_by: Amand 1945, pp. 53, 55-60 (Greek phrase appears verbatim in OCR, e.g. lines 485, 887, 3972, 4051, 4110, 4148, 4153, 4164)
note: Greek phrase only (a topos label, not a sentence). The full Greek formulation of the argument is preserved in Bardaisan via Eusebius PE VI.10 and in Sextus Adv. Math. V — NOT transcribed here verbatim (set found_verbatim:false if those sentences are wanted; the Amand OCR gives them in French paraphrase plus the Firmicus Latin block above).

text: MYRIOI / collective-death Greek formulation: the brief asked for the «μύριοι» collective-death formulation. I searched the OCR; the only μυρίοι/μύριοι hit (line 27517) is in an unrelated Greek block (δεσποίνῃ παραδοὺς αἰκίζεσθαι, καὶ μυρίοις περιβαλεῖν...). Amand presents the collective-death argument in French paraphrase, and grounds it for the patristic witnesses in Eusebius PE VI (already in corpus as passage_eusebius_praep_ev_6_6_*). I therefore do NOT propose a verbatim Greek 'myrioi collective death' quote — found_verbatim would be false. The Carneadean root is Cicero De Div. II.47.97 (Latin) / Sextus Adv. Math. V.91-94 (Greek), neither verbatim in the Amand OCR at the points I read.

ORPHANED DOXOGRAPHIC collection_* NODES. Checked relevance to Amand. (1) collection_aetius_placita: Amand uses Pseudo-Plutarch De Fato and Aetius' Placita as Greek transmitters of the conditional-heimarmene / Middle-Platonist material (synthesis_amand1945_pseudo_plutarch_*). A weak 'source_for' edge from collection_aetius_placita to the Middle-Platonist conditional-heimarmene concept is defensible (see edge below). (2) collection_dox_graeci_diels (Diels, Doxographi Graeci) is the modern edition that prints both Aetius and the Vetusta Placita — it is the EDITION underlying collection_aetius_placita, so a 'contains'/'preserved_in' relation between them is the natural fix, independent of Amand. (3) collection_dk (Diels-Kranz) and (4) collection_ls (Long-Sedley) are NOT specifically drawn on by Amand (1945 predates Long-Sedley 1987 entirely; DK is for Presocratics, which Amand touches only in his pre-Carneadean lineage). I propose NO Amand-based edges for collection_dk / collection_ls — flagging that their orphan status is out of scope for this dossier and should be addressed by a doxography-specific wave.

rationale: Aetius' Placita (with Pseudo-Plutarch De Fato) is, for Amand, a Greek doxographic transmitter of the Middle-Platonist conditional-heimarmene (ἐξ ὑποθέσεως) doctrine that Nemesius ch. 37-38 criticises. Low weight — Amand cites Ps.-Plutarch more than Aetius proper.

Aetius' Placita is reconstructed and printed in Diels, Doxographi Graeci (1879); the Diels edition is the modern critical vehicle of the Placita. This fixes both orphans and is edition-level, not Amand-specific.
